I hope the
minister will not think I am rude, and that he will curb his impatience. I do not know whether I am on the right item. I want to ask about the collection of radio licence fees.
That is the next item.
Will the minister say a word as to the activities involved in the suppression of radio interferences which involves this amount?

There are a number of employees stationed at headquarters of the radio division in Ottawa, and staffs are located in twenty-four cities across Canada. Over and above that, there are forty-six specially equipped radio patrol cars maintained for the investigation of interference. As a matter of fact there is a continual demand for investigation of interference in various towns, cities and communities, and that is done. The investigators, with their radio patrol cars, first interview those who have reported interference. They test the 55946-185
Supply-Transport
radio to ascertain whether there is anything radically wrong with it. Most of the time they discover it is because of an oil burner or some radioactive instrument, be it medical, dental or the like, and the person with the offending instrument is asked to discontinue its use or purchase some scientific device that will suppress the interference. On the whole I think a very helpful and satisfactory service is being performed.

Item agreed to.
Radio division-
517. Issue of radio receiving licences-(transport department only), $705,340.
What is the reason for the increase of some $25,000?
The increase is $54,000.
What is the reason for it?
The increase is, first, because of salaries, annual and basic salary rate increases.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: The increase is $30,000.
I am sorry, I was looking at item 516. The increase is $30,846.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: We just saved you $24,000.

Keep on assisting me and I will not object. It is made up of $29,000 for increases in salaries, $500 for postage, the rental of a tabulator, and an increase in commissions to postmasters of $578, which makes $30,846.
Can the minister tell me what the revenue was from the licences issued?
The gross revenue from the sale of radio licences has been continually on the increase. For 1949-50 it is $5,143,000.
What is the net? That is the gross.
That is the gross revenue from the sale of licences. Commissions paid amounted to $331,652. Therefore the amount paid to the C.B.C. is the addition of $5,143,000 and $331,000 making $5,474,000.

Does the minister know how many radio receiving sets in operating condition there are in Canada? I might as well explain what I have in mind. Have you any idea how many people are using receiving sets in Canada compared with the number of persons who pay licence fees for the use of sets?

I can only answer that question in this way. The number of those who are owners of radio receiving sets and who have paid their licences is 2,177,445. There is no way of knowing accurately the total

Supply-Transport
number of radio receiving sets, but by means of spot checks carried out from time to time in various cities we think that this number represents about 95 per cent of the total number of receiving sets in the country.

Have you not a better method than that? There are publications which tell you the number of receiving sets sold in Canada in 1949, 1948, and so on. They are available and I assume you have them. I was wondering how the number of persons from whom licence fees are collected has kept pace with the sale of new radios. Of course some of them will be replacements but have you any idea as to that? For example, the exact number for television is available at any time, but have you made any comparison between the number of radio licence fees sold in 1948 and 1949 and the number of new radios purchased?

We have not, for the reason that there may be as many as five radio sets in one house. The only thing the department is interested in is to see that the $2.50 licence fee is collected on one of those sets. That is the case today in many homes. I do not say there is an average of five, far from it; but I think it is pretty safe to say that in most homes there are two, if not three, small sets. I am also told that some of the sets become obsolescent and the owners break them up, throw them away or dispose of them by other means. For that reason it is difficult to make an accurate check of the full number of sets in the country. The way we get at it is by spot checks and percentages; and, as I said, we think the percentage is about 95.
Would you tell me what a spot check is?
It is a check that is made by an officer of this division who would go into a number of houses, I suppose-
Take a city of one hundred thousand people. How many houses would he cover?

They would take several streets and go into a number of houses, and by that method ascertain the percentage of those who had sets who were paying the licence fee. The result of those checks in various parts of the country would give the percentage I mentioned. I am informed now that fifty thousand homes were checked by this spot method.

Out of how
many?
Well, all across the country.
But out of what total number of receiving sets?
Out of a total of 2,100,000, I think it was.
And is that check more intense in certain areas than in others? Take a city the size of Toronto. How many men have you working there, and how many in Edmonton doing this sort of work?
There would be about ten people in Toronto, four people in Edmonton, I suppose about fifteen in Montreal-

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: None in Calgary?
Twelve to fifteen in Calgary.

The minister should be grateful to the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre for again helping him out. Knowing something of the situation, however, I assure the minister that he needs even more than that number, because I know many people who do not pay their licence fees. That is the thing I am getting at.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: They will be taking you on the staff.
I am not a good snooper; that is the trouble. When the minister said they entered houses I do not think he quite meant that. They make inquiries; that is the kind of check, I suppose?
Yes.
They have no right to enter houses.
No. If somebody objects they have no right to insist.
I was merely trying to correct your language, not mine. Have you not a car which you can drive around the streets and which will tell you in what residences there are radios?
Yes.
I suppose that is how you determine where to go to make your inquiries; or perhaps it is done by telephone?
That is right.

The minister says he thinks it is about 95 per cent perfect, as far as the payment of these licence fees is concerned. I wish I were an optimist like that; but that statement is on the basis of the spot checks of homes, apartments and so on?

Oh, yes. I made it quite clear that we could not have an accurate figure, and I told my hon. friend I could not possibly answer his question except in that way. It may not be the best method, but it is the one we follow as being most feasible.

I am not complaining about it. The department gets a list of sales of radios every month, does it not? Does anyone in your organization make a check and follow those radios to their ultimate resting places in the homes?
The dealers are required to make monthly returns to the department.
Does the department use those returns in calling upon people who have made purchases, to find out whether or not they have paid the licence fee, or does it rely only upon the spot checks?
I am told that it relies on both.
Do you compare the sales in a city the size of Edmonton, for example, with the number of licences issued? Do they bear any relationship?
I am told there is no relationship between the two.

A few moments ago the minister said $5,143,000 had been collected in radio licence fees. Then he was asked what the net amount was, and he said $331,000 was commission on those radio licences. Then he made the statement that the C.B.C. was paid $5,474,000.
That is right.
Then do we pay those commissions twice?
No, we pay them once.
Does not the man who sells the licence get a commission?
Yes, he does. That is covered in the vote.
If I may follow up that question, it would appear to me that the commission is paid twice.
If what the minister has stated is so, it seems to me the commissions on these radio licences are paid twice. They are paid once to the salesmen and once to the C.B.C.

The C.B.C. gets the full fee of
$2.50, which makes up the amount of $5,400,000 I gave a moment ago.

The minister said the C.B.C. was paid $5,474,000. That is the total of the fees collected and the commissions paid, is it not?
Supply-Transport

No; the C.B.C. gets $5,400,000, which is made up of $5,100,000 from the sale of licences and $331,000 in commissions. That has to be done by virtue of an amendment to the Canadian Broadcasting Act passed on July 17, 1947, under which the amount of commissions paid to issuers of licences and formerly deducted from the gross revenues payable to the C.B.C. now is paid out of the consolidated revenue fund.
How many radio licences were sold?
What was the total amount collected?

Then by paying the C.B.C.
$5,143,000 they are getting the full amount of the licence fee collected?
That is right.
Without paying the commission of $331,000?
That is right.

But the minister says the
C.B.C. gets $5,400,000?
Yes, they do; they get both.

On page 307 we have the explanatory note showing an amount of $375,000 as payment to the C.B.C. of the amount of commissions allowed issuers of licences. Is that part of the total of the $2.50 licence fees paid in Canada, or is it over and above that?
Yes, it is. It is the full amount of the commissions.
I know this is the full amount of the commissions; but is the C.B.C. paid the full $2.50 for all the licences in Canada, plus $375,000?
May I ask this question?
I want the answer to my question first.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Perhaps while the minister is getting the answer to that question I could advise the member for Saskatoon to ask his question.

I wanted to follow for a moment the line of thought the member for Calgary West embarked upon concerning radios which are newly purchased. I presume each radio which is imported from the United States is a subject for notification by the department of government concerned to the licensing branch of the Department of Transport. Is that correct?
55946-185^

Supply-Transport
I am informed that returns are made from the customs office to the Department of Transport.

I thought the Department of Transport was efficient in that direction, because when passing through the United States on my way home last summer I bought a car radio. As soon as I reached home I bought a licence for it from the transport division in my own city. Along about the time the snow fell last fall, I received a rather sharp letter from the department asking for some explanation of why I had not purchased a licence for imported radio No. so and so.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: You call that efficiency?

Just a minute. The letter said: If by any chance you have paid your licence for this thing, what is the number of your licence? I instituted a search in my home, and after a couple of days we found the receipt from the Department of Transport. I wrote a little note stating that I thought perhaps an explanation was due to me, and I gave them the number. I want to know what would have happened if I had been unable to find that particular receipt. The minister has not heard anything I have said.

I am trying to get an answer for the member for Macleod. I hope I have it now. The licensee pays $2.50 to the Department of Transport for a licence. We pay the full amount of the $2.50 to the C.B.C., which amounts to $5,474,707-I think that is the figufe I gave. The vendor commissions amount to $331,000, the amount I gave.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Is not the confusion created by the way it is worded on page 307, where it says that this payment is made to the C.B.C., the amount of commissions allowed issuers of licences? What is the amount on each individual $2.50 licence?
There is $2.30 paid to the department, and 20 cents paid to the vendor.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: In other words the C.B.C. gets $2.30 direct from the citizen, plus the 20 cents that is paid out of the $375,000 in this item?
I have nothing more to add to what I said a moment ago. I am trying to say that the C.B.C. gets $5,474,000. My hon. friend is putting it in another form, and he may be correct; I am not sure.
They get the full $2.50 and the department takes up the cost of sale.
That is right.

Could I have an answer to my question? I know the minister was not

listening, and I advised against the consideration of it while he was working out the other problem. If I bring a car radio into this country from the United States, notification of that importation is given to your department. I then proceed to buy a licence. Your department notifies me that I should buy a licence; that is what happened to me the last time; and if I had not been able to find my receipt to prove that I had bought that particular licence, what action could or would your department have taken? What protection have I?
Habeas corpus.
I become responsible for the mistake made by the department?
No, you become responsible for your own mistake-
Which was losing the receipt?
No, because the department keeps a duplicate copy of the receipt which was originally given, and the department will not proceed against the owner unless there is a breach of the act.

In that case, the next question is the obvious one: If the department had a receipt in the month of May, just after I got home from the session, why did they bill me for the licence in the month of November?
I presume my hon. friend has a particular case in mind.
Yes, my own.
I am afraid I cannot tell the hon. member why the department billed him. Probably they were in error; I do not know but that is possible.

When the department wrote to me and asked for an explanation, I wrote to them and told them the number of the licence and said I thought probably an explanation was due to me. It was not forthcoming. No attention was paid to my letter, so I thought I would get the explanation from the minister.
There is nothing like trying.
Could the minister tell me how many prosecutions there have been and what penalties have been imposed? What has been the total amount collected?
There have been 9,524 prosecutions.
Does the minister have the information by provinces?
Yes; British Columbia, 375; Alberta, 547; Ontario, 5,511; Quebec, 865; Nova Scotia, 795; New Brunswick, 195; P.E.I., 240.
What has been the cost to the department for these prosecutions?
The issue of licences and the collection of fees came to $306,000 for the term 1949-50.

The total amount of this vote appears to be $705,340. This is for the radio division, the issuing and collecting of licence fees. Are we to conclude that it cost $705,000 to issue and collect $5,143,000?

No; as I indicated at the
outset, this appropriation of $705,340 provides for salaries and other expenditures to the headquarters staff of the office here in Ottawa. The amount payable for the collection of licences is only a small portion of this vote. It is much less than half.
I was referring to the issuing and the collecting of licences.
Well, it covers headquarters staff and field offices engaged in the issuing of radio receiving licences. If there were no licences there would be no vote.
That is right; in other words, it does cost over $700,000 to collect these fees, because there would be neither office nor headquarters staff if we were not collecting radio licence fees.
The answer is yes and no. It does cost $705,000 to administer the branch, but to collect the licences, alone, it does not cost that much.

It costs about 14 per cent,
roughly, to collect them?
We worked it out last year at 12 per cent.
It is a little more this year, so it would be probably 13 per cent.

And there is a little more
revenue, too.

Would the minister give us
the number of licences issued for automobiles and trucks? I am referring of course to licences for radios in those vehicles. Are they kept separate, or is there any separation in that respect?
I think we can get that figure for the hon. member.

And, while you are getting it, may I ask what arrangements you have with
Supply-Transport
the post office department in paying commissions to them for the collection of fees. Is that paid in bulk, or is it paid separately?
It is 15 cents for one licence, instead of the 20 cents to the ordinary vendor.
And is it paid in bulk or sent separately to the different post offices across Canada.
Many of the post offices get books in advance. They return them, with the ordinary returns, to the post office; and there is a refund in that manner.

Then the main Post Office
Department here handles the whole thing for you; is that correct?

Only the staff post offices
do that.
And the other post offices receive them direct?
Yes.
What about the car licences?
Could we carry this item, and permit me to give that information as we go along?

In collecting these licences the Post Office Department does some of the work, and there are returned soldiers and others who make collections. Very often there is a time limit imposed in respect of the date at which the licences should be obtained. However, a good many people wait until the returned soldier or some other person, who has been in the habit of making the collection, comes around. Many people do not know whether to go to the post office or whether they could wait for the returned soldier. Is there any co-operation between the two, or are any instructions sent out in that connection?

There is the advice that goes out over the radio prior to the first of April. People who have radios will learn that licences are due in that way, because the notice is broadcast many times as the hon. member probably knows. These broadcasts indicate when licence fees are payable. It is at that time that the returned man who is a vendor begins his canvass. However, if the ordinary licensee wishes to purchase at the post office, I suppose there is nothing to stop him doing so.

But is any encouragement given to the returned man? It is a personal matter with me, because I might say my wife always wishes to purchase from a returned soldier, but he does not get around until after the time has expired.

Supply-Transport
The encouragement given is that he gets 10 cents more than the post office gets.
I always receive a brown card about so long and so wide telling me that my radio licence fee is due. Are those sent to everybody, or only to people in arrears?
I am informed they are sent to everyone who had a licence in the previous year.

How much does that cost,- because it seems to me that if canvassers are going around to sell these licences it is a waste of money to send out these cards to those who had licences in the year before.

The card has been very effective, and that is why we use it. It helps very materially in increasing the revenue, because, as the committee will see, the revenue has been increasing considerably from these sales. I cannot give the cost separately, but it is covered in this amount of $705,340.
In listening to all these figures I have become confused about these radio licences. As I have it now there were two million and one licences sold.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
I believe the figure was
2,100,000.
Oh, it was 2,100,000 was it? At $2.50 that gives something over $5 million, and yet the C.B.C. got $5,474,000.
There are a number of battery sets for which the fee is only $2.

Item agreed to.
Radio division-
518.	Telegraph and telephone service, administration, operation and maintenance, $1,354,845.
Why is this item, which deals with telegraph and telephone service, in the radio division estimates? Is it out of place?
I think not, because it is a form of telecommunication. In the department we find radio, telephone, telegraph-
Any teletype in there?
If I am wise, the answer is no. That is the only explanation I can give. It is a form of telecommunication.
In other words, it has nothing to do with radio?
No.
Although it is under that heading.
That is right.
What are those telephones and telegraphs? From where do they run?

They run throughout the country. They are services for isolated areas which could not provide telephone services for themselves unless some company were assisted. So to come to the assistance of points in the eastern part of Canada, Newfoundland, the maritimes and out on the west coast and on the Gaspe peninsula we provide the services and we operate them. The Minister of Public Works says, "also in British Columbia".
Does the department get any revenue?
Oh, yes.
Where does it appear?

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: It goes into the pot.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Study the public accounts and you will know the answer; do your homework and you will find out.
The expenditure for the last fiscal year was $1,130,000; the revenue was $498,000.
The total figure here for last year is $1,331,000. The minister gave the figure of $1,130,000.

Yes, I gave the expenditure for the last fiscal year. That is the estimate for this fiscal year. The hon. member asked me what amount of revenue was received. I say that last year the revenue received amounted to $498,000. I cannot tell what it will be this year because I will not know until the end of the fiscal year, but the estimate is about $500,000.
The estimate last year was $1,331,060 and the expenditure was $1,130,000. The department spent the sum of $200,000 less than the amount estimated for.
I am informed the reason is that we were unable to secure all the material and equipment which were necessary to put up the lines and the extensions.
Where is the other $200,000? Did it go back into the consolidated revenue fund, or does it show in these accounts?
Any revenue that is received is paid into the consolidated: revenue fund.
It just remains there. But where does it show in these accounts? I do not see where the unexpended $200,000 appears.
Of course, these are not accounts; they are estimates of expenditure for the next fiscal year.

However, quite frequently in some of these departments I see an unexpended appropriation not required. For instance, veterans affairs on the very next page, shows: "Appropriation not required for 1950-51, $10,000." You see the same thing right through the estimates. Why was not the $200,000 which was not required last year shown in the same way?
That is known as a revote and appears from time to time in the estimates. We have had several of them in these estimates.

This particular item of
$200,000 is the one I am asking about. Why does it not appear as an appropriation not required in 1949-50?
There is an item under radio division which reads: "Appropriation not required for 1950-51, $350,000."
I did not notice it before. Is the $200,000 part of that?
Where is that $350,000?
Right at the bottom of the page.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: That was last year.
What page are you reading from?
Page 63. It appears in italics at the bottom of the page.
If my hon. friend is referring to item 519, that is for construction and improvements.
No; just below that. It appears in italics, "Appropriation not required."

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is just for the purpose of comparison.
I am informed that this was to cover projects that we were not able to carry out, projects which because of the time element it was not possible to complete, and some which were overestimated.
I presume the revenue of $498,000 was put into the consolidated revenue fund.
Yes.
You get no credit in your estimate for that.
No, none whatever.
This afternoon the minister said that his department covered all telephones outside Ottawa; that is correct?
That is correct.

That is, in public buildings throughout, outside Ottawa?
Supply-Transport

No; this vote covers services, communication services to remote areas, sparsely settled sections of the country. This does not cover the cost of telephone bills; it is for service, telephone lines which are extended or constructed in remote areas, and would have nothing to do with the cost of government telephones to Vancouver or Edmonton. They are covered separately.
Can the minister explain the increase in this item for telephones, telegrams and postage from $14,600 to $126,500?

Under the public works system of accounting, this amount was provided for under the rentals primary to cover the payment of charges levied by commercial communication companies for detachment, maintenance and attendance of departmental telephone and telegraph facilities. The amount of $100,000 is involved between Prince George and Prince Rupert, which is paid to the Canadian National Telephone Company; and the remainder is accounted for by a large number of small cases of a similar nature across Canada, which makes up the $111,900.
It is a capital expenditure. It will not occur in another year. It is for work that is being done.
No; I am told it is a recurring vote.

I do not want to load the Minister of Transport with all the difficulties in the government telegraph service, because after all he has been doing that job only recently. It always seems to me that the government telegraph service has been one of the orphans of the department, that we have had in Ottawa. I have been wondering whether any active objective thinking has been done about the future of the government telephone service. It has often seemed to me that these land lines that we run into the government telephone service have reached a stage where they are now pretty well obsolete. I have been wondering whether the minister or his department had given any consideration to the substitution of radio telephones for those old galvanized wire lines that we run through some of the rougher sections of Canada, which I know are very expensive and very difficult to maintain.
There is another point that comes to my mind. I go into towns and I find that they are well serviced with Canadian National, Canadian Pacific and the government telegraph services. This government telegraph service was founded for the purpose of serving communities that had no other means of communication. I was wondering whether there was any possibility of eliminating any of the

Supply-Transport
offices and probably substituting radio telephone service in areas where it is necessary for the government to provide communication. It would not be necessary to have this service operated by the government telegraph operators as I believe a considerable amount of money could be saved by subsidizing private radio stations who would serve the public when necessary. I believe there is a great opportunity to save money here. I know the minister cannot look after all these things himself but perhaps he will instruct his officers to go to work on this matter of government telegraph services and see if a more efficient service cannot be substituted for it.

It is true that in some of the outlying districts the service is not what it should be, but it is far better to have a poor service than to have no service at all. I had a visit some two weeks ago from a gentleman from Labrador and he told me that the service there was terrific. That service covers 800 miles along the north shores of the St. Lawrence river and gulf and there is a reason for the type of service that is given. On the other hand, the service along the northwest staging route and the Alaska highway is a pretty efficient service. I have seen it in operation and it is modern and up to date.
We would like to see private or municipal corporations take over these services as we do not like to operate them at all. We do this as a service to the public. Where the population is not very dense we do not like to expend too much money, but following the suggestion of the hon. member for Comox-Alberni it may be possible to give consideration to providing a uniform method which would be up to date and more modern.

There is another matter which does not come under this item specifically and I ask the indulgence of the house in taking it up at this time. In the Quatsino district the minister's department chartered a boat from a certain individual at the rate of $4 per day and promised to pay that rate until it was returned. However, it seems that the man in charge of the boat got up one night and was looking around with a match and it blew up. It was a most unfortunate circumstance. The minister's department consulted the Department of Justice who said that there was no legal responsibility. That may be true in the strict legal sense, but the treasury board is now considering a submission from the department. I would be grateful if the minister would take a personal look at this to see if some fair settlement cannot be made.
1 shall be glad to do that.

521.	Steep Rock mines-construction, $62,000.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
I should like to deal with this and the following item together.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
For the last two or three sessions when these items were called I confined myself to asking questions, so as to get what information I could about Steep Rock. In addition I have had some questions on the order paper this year and a notice of motion for the production of papers as a result of which I have been able to get a fairly complete picture of this whole matter.
At the outset let me say that I recognize the urgency that obtained in the middle war years with respect to the production of iron ore and making as much of it available as possible, but it does seem to me that the practice which was instituted then has been carried forward a lot longer than it should have been.
When the figures are added together we are paying quite a bit to subsidize and assist this private corporation. I point out further that what we are assisting Steep Rock Iron Mines Limited to do is not only to mine ore in that very interesting body which was found at the bottom of Steep Rock lake but also to transport it to another country for smelting and fabrication. It raises the whole question whether we should not be using the iron ore in Canada rather than sending it to the United States and then buying it back, thus paying out good money in that way when we might be building up more industry in Canada.
As I understand the situation, an agreement was made involving the government, Canadian National Railways and in effect Steep Rock Iron Mines Limited, a private company which I believe is owned in the United States. The basic terms of the agreement are that in the first place the government would pay to the Canadian National Railways all the money required by them to build a spur line and certain other facilities from Atikokan, Ontario, to the Steep Rock mines. It is a short distance but at any rate considerable facilities had to be built there. In addition, Canadian National was to build a dock at Port Arthur so that the ore could be removed from the cars that brought it to Port Arthur from Atikokan and put on boats to take it across the lakes to the United States. As I say, the first term in this whole arrangement was that the government would pay the entire cost of constructing the facilities at Atikokan and Port Arthur.
It is noted that one of the other terms of the agreement is to the effect that the Canadian National Railways pays back to the government 6 cents on each ton of ore that
Supply-Transport
it transports, for the purpose of repaying the capital expenditures. I note immediately that to date well over $3 million has been spent by the government in construction expenditures and under the 6 cent per ton arrangement we have received from the Canadian National Railways only $239,000. Even at that, when one thinks of money that we are receiving from the Canadian National Railways one has to face the fact that the railway operates at a deficit, and therefore we are paying the money anyway. In the long run the picture is clear that we are paying in full for the extra facilities necessary between Atikokan and Steep Rock and at Port Arthur to make possible the shipment of iron ore from Steep Rock to the United States.
Another phase of the agreement related to the cost of shipping the ore from Steep Rock to the United States. During the war Canadian National indicated that it would cost a certain figure per ton to ship the ore. It was more than the company felt they could afford to pay and accordingly, because it was necessary to move the ore while the war was on, the government agreed to pay Canadian National Railways a subsidy of 20 cents per ton. When I have asked these questions of the minister it has always been pointed out that the money was not paid to Steep Rock Iron Mines Limited but to Canadian National Railways. Obviously it is as broad as it is long. By paying the 20 cents per ton to the Canadian National Railways out of government funds the government saves Steep Rock Iron Mines Limited that amount.
In addition, during the first year or so of the production of iron ore at Steep Rock, during the war when it was thoroughly defensible, it so happened that it was not possible to get the dock completed at Port Arthur, and other means had to be used to ship the ore to the United States. Instead of going to Port Arthur it went through Duluth, which meant that the freight was higher than it would have been going across the lake. Instead of the government having to put up 20 cents per ton to subsidize the freight the agreement indicates that the government put up 70 cents per ton. When one reads the agreement more closely, however, he finds that even the 70 cents per ton did not fully make up for the difference between what it cost to transport the ore and what Steep Rock Iron Mines Limited was paying. There was another 38 cents, and the agreement simply says that Canadian National Railways agreed to absorb that amount. I come back again to the fact that the Canadian National has a deficit and we pay for it out of the consolidated revenue fund. Therefore we paid out of public funds a total amount of $1.08 per ton during the first year or two.

Supply-Transport
I want to say again, and let there be no doubt about it, that one has no complaint about that practice being followed during the war years. The reason for it was set out clearly in the orders in council initiating this policy. We discussed it at the time and agreed with it. As a matter of fact it is good to know that tremendous body of iron ore was found at the bottom of Steep Rock lake. It is a most interesting mining operation. As hon. members probably know, the lake was drained, and for the most part the mining consists of huge electric shovels simply removing the overburden and then scooping up the ore body from the bottom of the lake. As I say, during the war it was obviously desirable that there should be these subsidies to make sure that the ore would be produced and made available for war purposes, but it is still being carried on.
Every year since the war there has been a vote for construction purposes and also a vote for the subsidy on freight. We are now paying a subsidy of only 20 cents per ton, and the amounts for construction that we are continuing to pay are small, but surely it is clear that what we are now doing is to render considerable financial assistance to a private corporation mining a very valuable natural resource and shipping it in its raw state out of the country for smelting and fabrication in the United States. It seems to me that the policy is all wrong, that if we are going to allow a private corporation to exploit this natural resource and ship it to the United States they at least should pay the whole cost of shipping it there, and we should not have to continue to pay the 20 cent subsidy. If they cannot do it that way then I suggest that here is an excellent opportunity for the development of another industry in this country.
I said earlier that one of the ways in which I was able to get the information which I have been giving the house was by means of questions and so on on the order paper. I ask hon. members to note in particular the answers found in sessional paper No. 171. That return was tabled in this house on Monday, April 24 of this year, and gives detailed answers to the questions I had placed on the order paper. One answer in considerable detail gives the actual amounts spent under the heading of construction expenditures right from the first year, 1944, down to the latest figure for 1950. I have added them up, and they total $3,168,142.13. We have paid that entire amount out of the consolidated revenue fund, and tonight we are asked to vote another $62,000 for construction purposes.
I have already said that there was in the agreement a provision whereby the Canadian

National Railways pays back to the consolidated revenue fund at the rate of 6 cents per ton on the ore it transports, but in the end the Canadian National gets that money from the consolidated revenue fund anyway. In addition to that $3,168,142.13 we have spent under this heading already, we have spent another considerable amount of money in subsidizing freight rates with respect to the shipment of that ore. The minister pointed out to me last year that we pay that money to the Canadian National; but we save it for Steep Rock Iron Mines Limited. During the time the subsidy was 70 cents per ton, which was during the years 1944-45 and 1945-46, we paid a total of $258,802.86. That, of course, did not include the 38 cents per ton absorbed by the Canadian National, which we had to pay, and which would amount to another $125,000 or $130,000. In addition to that $258,802.86, we have paid a subsidy since then at the rate of 20 cents per ton, to a total of $796,991.24.
If those two larger amounts are added they come to $1,055,794.10, and in a few moments we will be asked to authorize another amount of $129,066. Just to put those figures in round numbers, they add up to this; that we have paid out $3 million in construction expenditures and over $1 million in subsidizing the shipment of this natural resource out of the country. I have made it pretty clear already, but I should like to make it crystal clear that we had no objection to this being done during the war. But the war has been over for five years, and it does seem to me it is hard to explain a policy under which we keep on subsidizing a private corporation and assist it not only to exploit a raw material in this country but to ship it out of the country at the expense of the people of Canada.
The Depuiy Chairman: Shall the item carry? Carried.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Has the minister no comment to make on this Steep Rock question?

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Apparently not.
I was expecting the minister to say something; otherwise I would have asked a question.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Then may I ask a question. What is this $62,000 for construction purposes to be spent on?

The $62,000 is for the construction of 3,000 feet of trackage in the hill yard, required to handle possible increased production from the mine to cost $37,000; for strengthening the ore dock pockets with special lining for handling lump ore, $10,000; the purchase of land, $2,000; engineering

expense and surveys and development of plans for additional trackage facilities, $10,000.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: That is exactly the point I am trying to make. This sort of thing was defensible from 1942 to 1945, but is it defensible today to keep on spending money in this way, on facilities which are used for one purpose only? No one else uses that spur at Atikokan. Nobody else uses that ore dock at Port Arthur. It is this corporation we are helping by this item.

The point is quite simple. There are only two matters concerned here, and I do not believe the points made by my hon. friend are well taken. Referring to the subsidy in the first place, that was covered by an agreement during the war years under which the subsidy would be paid until such time as five million tons had been delivered. When the five million tons have been delivered the subsidy will cease. Thus far
4,354,000	tons have been delivered, so the subsidy will not have long to run. That is being done by virtue of an agreement, and I am sure the house would want that agreement to be carried out.
With reference to the acquisition of equipment, that too is covered by an order in council to which my hon. friend has referred. It is a fact that some $3,200,000 has been made available to the Canadian National Railways, which has benefited by it; but by virtue of that agreement the Canadian National have undertaken to pay back that amount by way of amortization, at the rate of 6 cents per ton. It is true that this may take some time, but the agreement is there and the government has safeguarded its interests in the money expended by the six-cent provision.
This was done at a time when ore was necessary, in a time of war. The bargain was well received in the house; in fact I can remember the speeches made by the former member for Davenport, who felt that the government was not going far enough in its expenditures in order to assist the movement of that ore from Atikokan and Port Arthur.
If the minister will permit me, I think what the former member for Davenport was supporting was the devolpment of an iron mine in Canada. That was his plea.
Yes; and he was insisting-
It was not a case of urging that it be all shipped out.

I am not saying that. He was urging that we were not going far enough in the matter of expenditures. There was
Supply-Transport
no question about that. On one or two occasions he felt that we should go further in assisting the development of the mine by way of capital expenditures. This money does not go to a foreign corporation; it goes to our own Canadian National Railways. There is nothing abnormal about it. We are bound to do this by reason of contracts entered into during the war years. As I say, the subsidy is about ended, and as far as the other expenditures are concerned we will receive our money by way of amortization.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: I recognize that the subsidy will end when five million tons have been shipped, but the Canadian National will have to continue to pay back the 6 cents per ton on the construction costs, even though it will not be getting that subsidy any more. When we realize that those construction costs amount to more than $3 million and that to date the Canadian National have paid only $239,000, it is apparent that the Canadian National will be paying that 6 cents per ton for a very long time. As far as we are concerned it is just taking it out of one pocket and putting it into another. We will pay the Canadian National deficit so they can pay this 6 cents per ton and pay back the cost of the construction work. Now, the minister talks about the way in which the whole business was conducted during the war years, but many of the contracts made during the war were renegotiated. We had some talk about that this afternoon. It seems to me that what we should have done long ago, was to recommend that the capital expenditure be considered a war expenditure and written off as such. We are not under any moral obligation, once the war is over and the emergency power act is no longer in effect, to continue subsidizing in the way we are.

Can the minister say whether there is any power in the contract to insist that the ships in which the ore is carried from Port Arthur across the lakes be Canadian ships? If so, are there any Canadian ships to carry it?
No, we have not the right to insist that it be carried in Canadian ships. There are Canadian ships for the carriage of the ore.
Does the minister know whether it is actually being carried in Canadian ships now?
I am not able to give that information.

I suggest he look into that, and even if it is not in the contract, surely we are in a position to bring some moral pressure to bear in order to ensure that we

Supply-Transport
at least get that much out of it, that the ore be carried in Canadian bottoms across the lakes.
I shall look into it.
Why cannot this ore be used in Canada instead of shipping it to the United States? This is a promising mine, and production is increasing all the time.

I gave the explanation for that last year, and it is as follows: Approximately 92 per cent of the ore is exported to the United States, and the balance is used by Canadian companies. The reason why it cannot be used here is as follows: The production of various types of steel requires ores of varying analyses, and it is believed that Canadian steel producers are using all of the domestic ores which their type of steel production will allow. The production of malleable pig iron at Port Colborne is being increased, and this is expected to increase the consumption of Steep Rock ore by about 35,000 tons. The ore imported from the United States is a type not produced by Steep Rock mines, or not produced in sufficient quantities to meet Canadian requirements.
How much is being exported to the United States?
I said 92 per cent.
No, in tonnage, what is the tonnage being exported to the United States?

The last estimate I have is
1,132,000	tons in 1949-50, so there would be 92 per cent of that. It has been increasing from the beginning, because in 1945-46 there were only 128,000 tons.

Item agreed to.
Board of Transport Commissioners for Canada-
524.	Board of Transport Commissioners for Canada-administration, maintenance and operation, $624,800.

This item refers to the board of transport commissioners, and I think it should stand.
Item stands.
Canadian maritime commission-
525.	Administration, $190,170.

This is the administration item for the Canadian maritime commission which body, as members know, was set up to advise the government on shipping and shipbuilding policy. In fact, they have charge of the shipping and shipbuilding of Canada. I have no intention of going into this policy in 
detail this evening, but there are three questions I should like to place before the minister.
The first one has to do with the need for Canada to build fast, modern cargo vessels. The other day when the minister was speaking of the ship construction that is being undertaken in Canada, I believe he gave the figure of $67 million over the next five years for construction for the government. At that time I asked him whether any of these fast cargo vessels were being built in any of the shipyards in Canada. His answer was no. I submit, Mr. Chairman, that that situation is very serious for Canada. It is a tragedy that we have not yet begun to build these fast cargo vessels.
I should like to refer to the report of the Canadian maritime commission, which is dated June 30 of last year. This was the report which summed up the history of shipping and shipbuilding in Canada, and made detailed recommendations as to what policy should be adopted. Throughout the report we find references to the need for fast cargo vessels; that was one of the main recommendations. In effect, the commission found that Canada must build fast cargo vessels if there was to be a Canadian merchant marine. For example, on page 20 we find this statement:
For the second time in twenty-seven years a Canadian government was faced with the problem of what to do with a large number of merchant ships acquired through the exigencies of war.
The report is there referring to the position after the recent world war.
Then it goes on:
The ships were of standard types designed to meet a wartime emergency. Their high fuel consumption, slow speed, and lack of refrigerated space unfitted them to hold their own against fast, modem, more economical cargo-liners which shortly after the war began to appear in British and foreign merchant fleets. It was obvious that, once the world-wide shortage of shipping had been overcome, the ships would not be able to compete with more efficient foreign vessels.
Then the report continues as follows:
Undoubtedly, the proper course was to replace the ships, and to that end, on the advice of the commission, the government evolved a replacement which is outlined later in this report.
At pages 32 and 33, we find this statement:
During the past year we have investigated the characteristics of Canadian ships employed in our shipping services, and have come to the conclusion that for many trades the standard war-built types now in operation are becoming inadequate. British and foreign cargo ships of post-war design are on the average one-third faster, are equipped with more efficient cargo handling gear, and are more economical to operate.
Then on the following page, this appears:
However, aside from the special requirements of individual shipowners, we believe that the type of

vessel most suitable for employment in our trade should have a service speed of at least 141 knots and a capacity of 7,500 to 10,000 deadweight tons. It should be designed for the carriage of deck cargoes and have a reasonable amount of refrigerated space.
Of course, that is not the type of ship that was built during the war.
Is that a cruising speed or a surface speed?
Carried.

I would suggest to the hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard, if he is in a hurry, to go back to Vancouver. He can perhaps do more good there than he does here. I can tell him that this item will not be carried until I have made my statement on it. I suggest that he might take a little interest in this question too, because it is one of vital interest to Vancouver.
You worry about yourself.

I am worrying about Canada, but you do not seem to be. The orders the government is giving for the building of ships amount to about half this figure of $28 million. The question is: From where is the other shipping construction to come? The shipbuilders of Canada apparently are very much worried about the situation. They say they simply cannot keep up the minimum number of employees set by the Canadian maritime commission, unless there is an increase in ships being built in Canadian yards. They suggest as one means of bringing about this increase the adoption of a policy whereby Canadian coastal trade shall be restricted to Canadian vessels, meaning vessels built in Canada. That policy would seem to me to be sound, although the minister may have reasons for considering it otherwise. I would ask him to tell the committee whether or not the government has any policy in mind which will make it probable that we will have

Supply-Transport
in Canada the construction of shipping at least to the value of $14 million a year, apart from government construction.
Then, the third question I would ask the minister is with regard to the rehabilitation of Canadian seamen who have lost their employment by reason of the shipping policy adopted last December. On October 15 last the number in the Canadian merchant marine had fallen to 4,100. That figure was contained in a return tabled on that date. I do not have the figure as of today, but no doubt the minister has it available.
I believe that each of these old cargo vessels carries a crew of about 35. The minister said the other day that since the policy was announced there have been 93 transferred to British registry, although I think 58 of those were actually being operated by the British under a wartime arrangement. He also said that there were transfers pending in respect of 23 more. That would make a total of 116 ships either transferred or to be transferred shortly to British registry. I would ask the minister to say how many men there are now in the Canadian merchant marine. Last night when we were discussing the question of merchant navy veterans he promised that he would tell us what the policy is with regard to helping these men, who are losing their jobs, to get new work.
I did not say that. I said that I would give the number of men who are affected by this movement, and it was not nearly as many as 5,000. That is not the same thing.

The 5,000 figure was a quotation from a press dispatch published in Vancouver in January, I think. I hope that the government has some policy to help in the rehabilitation of these men who are losing their work because of a change in Canadian shipping policy. These are the three questions I would ask the minister to deal with on this particular item.

The matters which my'hon. friend brings up are of considerable importance and perhaps I can give to the committee a comprehensive statement on the whole position because it affects the shipping policy of the country as a whole.
At the end of the last war Canada was left with shipping and shipbuilding industries of major proportions. These industries were revived as a result of the second world war. We were faced with the problem as to whether these industries could or should be maintained in Canada and if so, by what method. The government therefore at the end of 1947 created the Canadian maritime commission to advise it on this problem.

At the beginning of 1948 there were 215 dry cargo vessels which had been built by the government for war purposes and which had been sold to private Canadian operators and were engaged in the deep-sea trade. They were sold on the condition that they were not to be transferred out of Canadian registry without consent of the government.
At that time deep-sea operations were profitable and all these ships were fully employed. In spite of the fact that Canadian costs were the second highest in the world, the freight market was high enough to offset such costs.
In February, 1948, the maritime commission, having had an opportunity of making a survey of world shipping conditions, advised us that in its opinion the freight market was bound to decline and that Canadian ships would become uncompetitive. The government therefore adopted the so-called replacement plan whereby owners were permitted to sell vessels from time to time provided that the proceeds were placed in an escrow account to be used for shipping purposes.
The reasoning underlying the replacement plan was that Canadian operators bought the ships from the government at reasonable prices and terms. In these circumstances it was felt reasonable that operators instead of selling out at a profit should use such profits for the purpose of remaining in the shipping business. It was also felt that if the commission's forecast of falling freights were correct it would be better to have money in the bank rather than have ships laid up and rotting at their anchors for lack of employment.
At the time this plan was brought into effect the sale market for vessels was high. The plan was welcomed by Canadian operators. As a result 44 vessels have been sold to date at a gross sales price amounting to about $27 million which has been paid into the escrow account.
Although the escrow account has only been in operation for little over a year the sum of $4,249,430 has been or is being used for the purpose of replacement, conversion or improvement.
There follows a breakdown which will take some time to go into, but the amount, as I said, is $4,249,430 for the purposes of replacement.
It will be seen that the operation of the plan is already affording work to Canadian shipyard labour. There is of course a much larger volume of work in the shipyards to which I will refer in a moment, but the escrow

fund is being used to encourage work which would not otherwise take place. I am not anxious to see the escrow fund used up too quickly as it will form a backlog of employment in the future.
As well as affording work for Canadian shipyard labour the escrow fund has enabled Canadian ship owners to consolidate their holdings. Owners are permitted to borrow from such fund to discharge mortgages on their ships. To date about $8 million has been borrowed for that purpose. This is not only to the benefit of the government in that the government receives the balance of the purchase price of the ship which was secured by mortgage but it also enables owners to reduce their overhead by way of mortgage interest. Such borrowings are repayable to the escrow fund which is in effect a revolving building reserve.
In passing I think I should refer to a statement in the second annual report of the Canadian maritime commission which may have escaped the attention of the members of this house. When all mortgages are paid, the government will have recovered out of a total expenditure of approximately $270 million about $200 million out of the operation .and sale of vessels built by the government and placed under management of the crown-owned Park company. As the cost of these vessels was part of Canada's war expenditure, the sum of $200 million represents a very creditable recovery to the Canadian taxpayer. At the moment there is the sum of about $28 million outstanding on mortgages representing the balance of purchase price due to the government in respect of the sale of these ships. This balance is payable by instalments and I have no doubt it will be collected in full.
However, in order to maintain a nucleus of a Canadian flag fleet, and incidentally to collect such balance of $28 million, it has been necessary for the government to take the steps which I now propose to outline.
Before I leave the subject of the escrow fund, perhaps I may be permitted to refer to a question which the member from Van-couver-Quadra asked me a moment ago, namely, if any fast cargo ships were being built in Canada at the present time and my answer is "no." I assume that he refers to dry cargo vessels with a speed of over 15 knots. I have no doubt that he had in mind the usefulness of such vessels in the event of war.
If a war should occur, we will of course need ships of all kinds and sizes. Much would depend on the nature and scene of any future war in determining what shipping services
Supply-Transport
would be required. Nevertheless it is necessary to make plans in peacetime to meet any emergency which may occur. I do not think that 1 am committing any breach of confidence in saying that discussions are now taking place between north Atlantic treaty nations for the purpose of pooling their shipping resources in the event of war. It will, I am sure, give satisfaction to the members of this house to know that Canada has played some part in the idea of creating an allied shipping pool. In the event of war the creation of such pool will make available to the member nations every variety of shipping service. For obvious reasons I am not giving any details, but I think I may say that Canada's contribution to such pool would consist at .the present time of almost 2 million deadweight tons of shipping. This is by no means an inconsiderable contribution.
Not only would Canada's contribution be large but it would also be useful. Canada's merchant fleet, consisting as it does mainly of Park vessels, affords a large bulk-carrying capacity. War would again necessitate the availability of a large number of bulk carriers. For instance a number of such ships would be required in the bauxite trade which would be one of the essential services to Canada in time of war. As far as bulk-carrying is concerned, Canada's fleet is not outdated or outmoded. It may perhaps illustrate my point when I say Great Britain now regards ships of this type strategically useful up to the age of 20 years. None of the Canadian-owned vessels is more than 8 years of age. As I have said, I do not propose to discuss this matter in detail except to say that the idea of present planning is to provide that ships of all types should be made available to member nations according to their needs.
In his statement to the house on December 9 last the Prime Minister mentioned these matters and also stated the government policy in respect of shipping. I do not propose to go over this ground again except to remind the house that in order to enable the Canadian flag fleet to operate competitively in the world market about $25 million in annual subsidies would be required. The government did not consider that an expenditure of this magnitude could possibly be justified. It was therefore decided to permit transfer of a number of ships to United Kingdom flag.
One of the major factors handicapping the Canadian flag fleet was its inability to carry cargoes yielding freight revenues in sterling. Expenditures being practically entirely in dollars it was necessary to find dollar

Supply-Transport
freights. Canadian owners were thus debarred for practical purposes from the large sterling freight market.
Under the arrangement which has been made with the United Kingdom, Canadian owners transferring ships to the United Kingdom flag will have free access to this market. Under such arrangements Canadian owners appoint agents in England who will receive the gross freights earned by such vessels whether such freights are payable in dollars or sterling. All ships disbursements are made through such agents and the United Kingdom will permit the net profit to be transferred to Canadian owners in dollars.
This arrangement is obviously advantageous to both Canada and the United Kingdom. The ships continue to operate under a commonwealth flag and have freedom of access to the sterling freight market. Gross dollar freights are paid into Great Britain which is in need of dollars and it is only the net profit in dollars which is repayable to Canadian owners, which should not put any drain on the British dollar supply.
Another feature of this arrangement should be mentioned. While the port of registry of these vessels is being transferred from Canada to the United Kingdom, the ownership is retained in Canada. In the event of an emergency Canadian owned ships operating under United Kingdom flag will either be returned to Canadian flag or will be treated as pant of Canada's contribution to the allied shipping pool. Canada's position in regard to shipping in the event of war is not being impaired.
As stated by the Prime Minister it was considered advisable to maintain some ships under Canadian flag during the period required for the planning of the allied shipping pool. It was therefore decided to devote for this purpose the sum of $3 million which is mentioned in the present estimates. We have been advised by the maritime commission that not more than this amount will be sufficient to keep about 40 ships operating under Canadian flag.
As I have pointed out on previous occasions the freight market has declined, especially over the period of the last year. This has been due to a variety of causes, not the least of which was currency devaluation which occurred in the latter part of the year. There has not been a corresponding drop in Canadian cost of ship operations. It is hoped that the assistance now afforded to Canadian flag operators will enable them to pass through the present difficult period. It is not unreasonable to expect that the freight market will rise from its present low level at least to some extent. In the meantime
[Mr. Chevrier.l
Canadian owners who transfer a portion of their fleets to British registry will be receiving revenues from those vessels. There is an opportunity to Canadian owners who desire to do so, and who show initiative and foresight, to maintain Canadian flag vessels in operation.
Prior to the coming into effect of the shipping policy, there were 40 Canadian vessels lying idle. I have no doubt that practically the whole fleet would have been laid up by this time if the government had not taken immediate steps to deal with the problem. Today there are only 12 out of 172 vessels laid up and I am confident that these will shortly find employment.
As I said last Friday there are 172 oceangoing dry cargo vessels owned in Canada which are subject to the flag restriction covenant. Of these, the owners of 93 have applied for permission to operate under British flag and such permission has been granted. Twenty-three applications in respect of transfers still are pending. It must be understood that the actual date of transfers will depend upon the position of ships from time to time. The transfers are being made on as gradual a basis as possible to avoid any great disruption of employment at one time.
The Canadian maritime commission has to date approved subsidies in respect of 31 ships and 9 subsidy applications are still pending. Applications for subsidies are granted on the basis of the subsidized vessels employing Canadian crews and the commission is choosing vessels which are the most economical to operate and which are likely to be able to maintain themselves in trades beneficial to Canada and strategically useful to Canada in time of emergency. Sixteen applications for subsidies have been declined on the basis that the vessels do not fall in these categories.
While there is no item in the estimates of the Canadian maritime commission dealing with shipbuilding, perhaps I may be permitted to refer briefly to the state of this industry. Devaluation has again had serious repercussions in that it has effectively put a stop to shipbuilding in Canada for export. Nevertheless I am glad to say that there are still
9,000	men employed across Canada in shipbuilding and ship-repairing. This figure is to be compared to the figure of 7,000 men which is the estimate of employment given to us by the maritime commission necessary to preserve the industry on a nucleus basis.
I am informed that the total dollar value of tonnage delivered in the year 1949 amounted to approximately $32 million, comprising 26 vessels aggregating 54,000 gross

tons. During the same period repairs and conversions accounted for an additional $18 million. Shipbuilding and ship-repairing in 1949 therefore amounted to $50 million. This can be compared to almost $107 million in 1948 and $68i million in 1947.
As I stated in the house on Friday, 5th May, the dollar value of shipbuilding in preparation or under construction in Canadian yards from all sources, that is domestic, export and government account amounts to more than $67 million. I should like to draw to your attention that almost 62 per cent of all shipbuilding on order is for departments of government including national defence. With the exception of the naval program, the ships now building for government account are needed replacements which were postponed during the war years.
That is for the five-year period?

Yes.
The present naval shipbuilding program accounts for approximately $34 million and is comprised of three antisubmarine escort vessels, four Influence type minesweepers, one gate vessel and one icebreaker. I think it is only fair to state, however, that with the exception of the icebreaker and the gate vessel which are now under construction, I am advised that shipbuilding will not commence on the balance of this program until the late summer of this year and that it will extend over a period of at least three years.
I can assure the house that every effort is being made by the Canadian maritime commission, with the wholehearted cooperation of all departments of government operating floating equipment, to plan and co-ordinate shipbuilding requirements extending into the next five years.
Present indications are that including the cost of the naval vessels which I have mentioned, estimated expenditures by the government in Canadian yards to meet the cost of necessary new construction and replacement for normal requirements over the next five years will exceed $60 million.
Then with reference to the question of employment, the Canadian maritime commission estimates that not more than 1,500 potential jobs will be lost to Canadian seamen by reason of the transfer policy. I make that statement prefaced by this additional statement: Half a loaf is better than no loaf at all. Had it not been for the policy announced by the Prime Minister all ships would eventually have been laid up. As it is now, most of the ships are transferred to United Kingdom registry and 42 ships are now under Canadian registration.

I think I should be allowed to complete the statement because after all the hon. member asked three questions and here we are at the end of Friday evening and my estimates are still before the committee. If I had been given a little more time I could have made this statement earlier. I had hoped I could complete my estimates tonight, but unfortunately I shall not be able to do that.
As I say, the Canadian maritime commission estimates that not more than about 1,500 potential jobs will be lost to Canadian seamen by reason of the transfer policy. These men will not all be thrown out of their jobs at once but will lose them gradually as the transfers proceed. They may choose to rehabilitate themselves through vocational training or may possibly secure employment in the ships which are being transferred.
I am informed by the commission that Canadian owners who are transferring the operation of their ships to United Kingdom registry are doing their best to afford jobs to Canadian seamen who desire to stay in the ships. There is only one difficulty in this connection which I think I should mention quite frankly and that is that the British seamen's union is doubtful about taking Canadian seamen into its ranks. This is a subject which is under discussion at the moment.
I cannot blame the British seamen's union for its attitude. We are all aware of the disastrous effects of the communist-led strike of the Canadian seamen's union last year. I commend to every member of this house the reading of the white paper issued by the British government on this subject on the 14th of December last. As to the cause of this strike and its international inception and ramification I cannot do better than read from the foreword of the white paper written by the British minister of labour:
A review of the circumstances in which these strikes started and spread makes it clear that preparations for the strikes began as early as the latter part of last year, although the first strike did not take place until May of this year. The evidence shows that there was throughout a cold and deliberate plan, and that the unofficial leaders were completely indifferent to the loss and suffering that might result. They had one aim and one aim only -to restore the fortunes of the communist dominated Canadian seamen's union. In the course of

the strikes they engaged in misrepresentation and violence and it was inevitable that when the trades union leaders in this country, mindful of the interests of their members, opposed the strikes and tried to bring out the true facts, they were in turn assailed and abused by the communists in this country who were supporting the strikes.
There is a lesson to be drawn from this unfortunate experience.
